Luneth's verdict was "good enough, but needs some refinement", and he closed the session there, so this is banked as a starting point and not approved as finished. He did not say what needs refining and I have deliberately not guessed. The next session must ask him before touching it. The work that mattered on this element happened before any markup existed. Sodium is where Wallach stands furthest from mainstream medicine, and the trap is that you can quote him into either position and both quotes are real. His 2015 book says salt does not cause high blood pressure and that restricting it will shorten your life. His own 1995 sodium toxicity table lists hypertension, edema, congestive heart failure and renal failure. A panel built on either sentence alone would misrepresent him. So one panel prints both lists side by side, unedited, and states inside the figure that the same author wrote them nineteen years apart. He does reconcile them, but only by moving the cause: he argues the salt sensitivity seen in high blood pressure comes from restricted calcium and potassium rather than from the salt. That reconciliation sits in the closing paragraph rather than being smuggled up into the headline, and every panel touching blood pressure or salt restriction carries a note saying plainly that this contradicts consensus and is not advice. Someone on a prescribed low-sodium diet for heart failure could land on this page, and the page should not read as permission. The other thing worth keeping is that I walked into a trap I had documented myself one element earlier. The salt block's ground shadow carried a plain opacity attribute on an element that the reveal animation forces to full opacity, so it rendered as a solid black oval - the identical defect I had fixed on the vanadium tubes, with my own warning about it sitting in the stylesheet I had just copied across. Knowing a trap and writing it down is not the same as not falling into it.   ↳ Seven header concepts for folic acid, and Luneth approved all of them on the first round. What is worth remembering from this one is not the design. Four days ago Luneth read the actual page of the 2014 book, we agreed it had misprinted that figure, and we deleted the claim rather than post a number he demonstrably rejects. Folate's target is 1,000 micrograms, from his own 1995 program. Had I taken the notes at face value, all seven panels would have carried the government's RDA as his recommendation. The same notes said the corpus holds 24 claims for folate when it holds 38, and stated flatly that no discovery or history material exists for this vitamin - while two of the strongest panels are built on precisely that history. This is now the third element in a row where a concept Luneth picked was built on material its own notes forbade. B2's glow, B5's yeast flask, and now B9's thirty-one-year FDA trail. One figure was making a false statement about its own picture, and there is no gate that can see that.   ↳ Three pieces of work closed together, and the third is the one that matters most. B5 (PANTOTHENIC ACID) -- FIVE OF SIX CONCEPTS PICKED The labelled-figure rule learned from B2 held on the first attempt: six concepts, five approved ("A, C, D, E, and F are all good"). A becomes-coenzyme-A (B5 -> CoA -> four unrelated jobs under named columns) - C body-vs-mood, the same deficiency list split into two lanes, every word his - D four doses drawn to one scale, the 4 mg RDA as a sliver, with a 100x hero to the overdose range - E found-by-accident, a labelled yeast flask and 1930s->1940 - F the quiet teammate, four programs at a near-constant dose. B (three books, one shared sign) was NOT picked, and the reason is worth keeping: "showing contradictions across books is not something to bring front-facing." The figure was built to show three books AGREEING on burning feet; he read it as three books disagreeing. He said explicitly not to make a rule of it, so it is recorded as a note. Two factual slips were caught before he saw them, both corrected toward the more conservative reading. D's headline claimed you would need "five thousand times" the RDA before Wallach calls it an overdose; his range is 10-20 g, so it BEGINS at 2,500x -- 5,000x is the top of the range, and putting the threshold there overstates how much is safe. In a dose context that is exactly where 00.A demands rigidity. C claimed burning feet sits "four words" from quarrelsome; the verbatim gives three. THE OVERLAP DASHBOARD -- ANSWERING AN UNANSWERABLE QUESTION HONESTLY Luneth noticed that many nutrients share deficiency signs (depression, mood) and worried a header would imply "THIS is the mood vitamin". He asked which nutrients are MOST responsible for which conditions, on a percentage scale, and flagged himself that this might not be derivable without hallucinating. He was right: Wallach assigns no percentage of responsibility to any nutrient for any condition, anywhere in the seven books. Inventing one would have been fabrication. So the dashboard derives the only thing that IS in the corpus -- how often he says it. Share of Wallach's own claims for a condition, split into cause (deficiency_sign) and cure (protocol), never summed, with book-breadth offered as the more honest signal. The distinction is stated in the largest type on the page. The headline finding is deflating and useful: only 11 of 542 conditions have three or more INDEPENDENT claims on both sides. Everywhere else a single protocol claim names a dozen nutrients at once and all of them score, so a "ranking" is really a membership list -- 356 of 365 cards say so explicitly, with the count of distinct source claims per lane. Least-specific signs: arthritis 45 nutrients, depression 31, headache 31, rheumatoid arthritis 30, dementia 28. Luneth's instinct was right and the problem is wider than mood. Design consequence: no header may imply one element owns a crowded sign. Verified by writing an independent recount of depression and checking it against the generator's output before shipping. THE DOSSIER SWEEP -- IT IS SYSTEMIC Three dossiers in a row had turned out to assert things that are no longer true, so rather than keep discovering it one element at a time, tools/dossier_sweep.py now audits all 47 against the sealed corpus. 25 of 47 cite at least one DEAD claim id. 44 of 47 understate their own claim count -- sodium says 14 where the corpus holds 66, vitamin-b12 says 37 against 75, vitamin-e 68 against 104. 42 carry a flat "this material does not exist, do not use it" assertion, and several are now false. The sharpest evidence: two concepts Luneth actually PICKED -- B2's "The glow that named it" and B5's "Found by accident" -- are built entirely on material their own dossier forbids as outside knowledge. CORRECTION TO THE RECORD: chronicle/next-chunk.md logged boron.md as CLEAN. It is not -- it cites the dead WAL-CLM-RARE-000098 and undercounts by 14. The old clean/dirty notes in the handoff are not trustworthy and have been replaced by a pointer to the sweep. vitamin-b9, the element chosen next, cites dead WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000123 and says 24 claims where the corpus holds 38. A guard was appended to chronicle/header-research/README.md so a future session runs the sweep before trusting a dossier at all. A dossier is a head start, never an authority. TOOLING tools/mockup_measure.js compared text against text only, so it passed a figure whose label read "sterols and steroid hormone|s" -- nothing overlapped it, it simply ran off the canvas. It now checks every label against its own viewBox edges and exits non-zero on a clip. ## 2026-08-09 20:15 UTC-05:00 · round-close · element-headers
B2 header approved at round 4 after three rejections. The lesson: a header figure must LABEL ITS OWN PARTS -- unlabelled mood art "literally says nothing". Found it by screenshotting the sets Luneth had already approved, instead of designing from taste a fourth time.
  ↳ Vitamin B2's illustrated header took four attempts. The first three were rejected, and the third rejection is the one that taught something. I had built five figures that were genuinely beautiful -- a field of lights guttering out, a crack splitting open, a glare washing out a room, a fluorescent glow breathing in the dark -- and Luneth threw all five out: "huge illustrations that literally say nothing ... it's there for no apparent reason. Illustrations MUST MAKE VISUAL SENSE." He was right. Every one of those figures was an atmosphere with no words in it; all the explaining sat in the text underneath, so the picture itself carried nothing. Rather than guess a fourth time, I opened the header sets he had already approved and looked at what they had in common. It was not subtle: every approved figure names its parts inside the frame. So the fourth round rebuilt all six figures that way, and he picked three of them. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY (r3, five concepts, all deleted) Unlabelled atmospheres: a dot-field "cell lights" wave, an abstract fissure, an optical glare bloom, a luminous whey glow, plus one typographic roster. Four of the five carried zero in-figure text; every label sat below the figure, disconnected. Diagnosis in Luneth's words: they "say nothing" and are "there for no apparent reason." THE RULE, DERIVED FROM EVIDENCE NOT TASTE Screenshotted temporary/awaiting-refinement/vitamin-b3-demos-r1.html and vitamin-b1-demos-r1.html. Niacin's NAD figure labels Carbohydrate / Fat / Protein going in and Energy coming out. B1's rice grain labels "thiamine-bearing bran" on a leader line, "POLISHING" on the arrow, and captions each grain. Niacin's three Ds label each letter with its word plus THE GUT / THE SKIN / THE MIND. The falsifiable test that falls out: could a reader get the whole panel from the figure alone, with the prose removed? If no, it is decoration. Corollary: he does NOT dislike diagrams -- the standing "diagram clutter" failure mode is about CLUTTER; a clean 5-node labelled flow is the approved genre. Also: restrained line art on the tan background, not 760px dark full-bleed slabs. r4 -- SIX LABELLED CONCEPTS, THREE PICKED A what B2 becomes (B2 -> FMN + FAD -> Energy under named columns) - B it switches the others on (two named conversions: inactive B6 -> functional B6, tryptophan -> niacin, each enzyme named on its arrow; NEW this round and the strongest unused idea) - C the three sites Wallach names, three across, each mark over its own name - D his 12-entry deficiency roster with depression and dizziness ignited - E the 1879 discovery: a dish of whey and its fluorescence, both labelled, over an 1879/1932/1935 rule - F clear lens vs clouded lens with the early eye signs named. Luneth: "C, E and F are the best." DEFECTS CAUGHT BY LOOKING, THAT NO PROBE REPORTS (1) a leader line running straight through its own caption -- the single most common rejection in this project -- fixed by rebuilding C as a three-across roster that needs no leaders at all; (2) a caption clipped at the SVG edge; (3) a caption whose last word sat behind a drawn vessel. All three were invisible to the text-vs-text collision pass and visible immediately in a screenshot. DOSSIER DRIFT -- SECOND CONFIRMED CASE chronicle/header-research/vitamin-b2.md carries two flags that are now false: it says the mechanism lives in claim_text with "no mechanism verbatim to pull by ID" (WAL-CLM-EPIGEN-000243 has a full quotable one, used in four panels), and it says the yellow-green pigment fact is world knowledge that must never be injected (WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000297 states it byte-exact, plus 1932 Warburg / 1935 Kuhn). Two in a row is a pattern, not a coincidence; flagged for a sweep. TOOLING -- A HOLE CLOSED tools/mockup_measure.js compared text against text only, so it passed a figure whose label read "sterols and steroid hormone|s" -- nothing overlapped it, it simply ran off the canvas. It now also checks every label against its own viewBox edges (right/left/bottom) and exits non-zero on a clip. ## 2026-08-08 16:43 UTC-05:00 · incident · element-headers/quote-treatment
Correction: I wrongly told Luneth I didn't change the quote styling - he proved a before/after. My demos (niacin, B1, B6) dropped the app's real .ds-pull-quote component for a plain border-left quote; my 'no change' compared to an already-regressed baseline. Record corrected.
  ↳ A correction to the record, and to what I told Luneth. He asked why I changed the quote styling in B6; I answered that I hadn't — that the standard quote was byte-identical to niacin and B1 and only the epilepsy concept deviated. He then showed a before/after screenshot proving I had changed it. He was right. This entry corrects the falsehood I stated and committed (the prior B6-rejection note, entry lg_mskw09hw_pcfv52). The truth: the established Wallach-quote treatment is the app's design-system component `.ds-pull-quote` — a large italic pull-quote carrying the giant opening-quote glyph (via ::before, in the accent colour), a `.ds-mark` warm-yellow highlight on the key phrase, a `footer` attribution reading "— DR. JOEL WALLACH · BOOK (ED. YEAR)", plus a "General education, not medical advice" disclaimer. It is rendered live by entity-page.ts and defined in design-system.css (.ds-mark at line 475, .ds-pull-quote at 749), documented in STYLE-GUIDE.md. My header demos — niacin, B1, and B6, and the mineral run before them — hand-rolled a plain border-left quote at about 1.04rem with a mono claim-id line, instead of that component. That is a real and visible regression. Why my answer was false, mechanically: I compared B6's quote only against niacin's and B1's. But those two had already abandoned .ds-pull-quote, so "byte-identical to niacin/B1" measured against an already-regressed baseline and confirmed a falsehood rather than catching it. Comparing to the wrong baseline is how I convinced myself nothing had changed. Fixes applied this session: corrected chronicle/next-chunk.md (the B6-retry note's quote diagnosis had it backwards — the plain quote IS the regression, not the standard) and appended a correction line to chronicle/build-log.md. No fragment files were reverted (all gitignored scratch; niacin and B1 remain banked as starting points, with the quote fix now logged as a refinement item for them too). Deeper lesson, and probably the real root of the "lower quality" Luneth flagged beyond the infographic-idioms point: build header figures with the real design-system components, not hand-rolled approximations of them. The retry, and the eventual refinement of niacin and B1, must use the real .ds-pull-quote + .ds-mark treatment.

## 2026-08-06 16:29 UTC-05:00 · milestone · gate/no_duplicate_questions
Shipped no_duplicate_questions (board 89 -> 90): two claims on one entity page can no longer ask the reader the same thing. Threshold-free, 29 known cases allowlisted in-gate with reasons that expire.
  ↳ The duplicate cards Luneth kept finding now have a machine that catches them, which is the only thing that actually ends this. Every previous pass fixed instances; the class survived because the detector was structurally blind to it. WHAT THE GATE ASKS. Not "are these claims similar?" -- that needs judgement and a threshold, and both drift. It asks the one question that is decidable: do two claims on the same entity page ask the reader the same thing? Bucket by subject and normalised question; a bucket with more than one claim is a violation. Normalisation lowercases, strips punctuation, drops a small stopword list and sorts the remaining tokens, so a reordered restatement still collides while genuinely different content words do not. No score, no tuning, nothing to drift. WHY A SECOND GATE INSTEAD OF FIXING THE FIRST. no_duplicate_claims puts the book inside its bucket key and additionally demands that one quote literally contain the other. Measured today, it cannot see 407 cross-book and 615 cross-facet candidate pairs. The vitamin D pair Luneth found by eye was invisible to it three separate ways. WHAT I REFUSED TO BUILD, AND WHY. The facet audit recommended extending the old gate to compare claims across facets inside one book. I measured that before accepting it: 28 pairs, and most are the legitimate pattern where one paragraph correctly answers a "What is X?" and a "What does X do?", or a catalog entry correctly feeds both a discovery and an etymology card. A gate that fires on 28 correct cases is noise, and noise trains people to ignore the board. Recommendation overridden on evidence, and the reasoning is written into the gate's own comment so nobody re-proposes it from the audit next month. THE ALLOWLIST HAD TO EXPIRE. 29 known collisions remain, and Luneth wants them cleared next session, so the gate ships with them listed. The dangerous version of that is a baseline entry, which is invariant-scoped and would forgive the entire class forever. Instead each group sits inside the gate with a written reason of one of two kinds: no honest split exists (one claim is a strict content subset of the other, or it is the same Wallach passage reprinted in two books), or it is genuinely distinct but its short answer must be re-cut before its question can move. And a carve-out that stops matching FAILS the gate -- so fixing a collision forces deleting its excuse in the same patch. The list cannot rot into an amnesty. That second category is the lesson from earlier today worth keeping. An agent can always invent a question that sounds distinct; 25 of 44 proposed re-cuts promised content that was in neither the answer nor the claim. Shipping those would have replaced a duplicate-looking card with one that lies about what it answers, which is strictly worse. So the rule is now explicit: a question its own card cannot answer is a worse defect than the duplicate it replaces. The negative test runs seven cases and the one I care most about is the one where the gate must NOT fire: the same question under two different subjects renders on two different pages and is not a duplicate. Two of the seven cases were wrong when I first wrote them -- one raised a TypeError because ** demands string keys, and one reused a real question that collided with an unrelated third zinc claim, a test bug wearing a gate bug's clothes. Both are fixed with the reason recorded in the file rather than quietly corrected. Board 90/90. Corpus untouched this round -- no seal, still 2,230 claims at version 469. Everything else Luneth listed is deferred to the next session by his instruction, so nothing hangs over the header demo work when we return to it.

## 2026-08-06 14:46 UTC-05:00 · round-close · corpus/full-defect-sweep
Swept every open corpus defect class at once after Luneth found duplicate cards on the vitamin D page. Root cause: the duplicate gate is blind three ways. 46 re-filed, 20 deleted, 2 fabricated doses caught.
  ↳ Luneth pointed at two cards on the vitamin D page saying the same thing and asked why duplicates keep surviving pass after pass. He was right to be angry, and the honest answer is that the gate meant to catch them could never have seen them. It compares claims only within the same book, only within the same section of a page, and only when one quote is a literal substring of the other. Two books wording the same fact differently miss all three tests. Every previous pass was fixing symptoms one at a time against a detector that was structurally blind. So this time nothing was fixed one at a time. Agents read the actual book pages for 1,021 candidate pairs, 71 same-source groups, 88 suspect figures and every OCR fusion in seven books, and every proposed deletion was handed to a second agent whose only job was to refute it. THE RESULT WAS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT I EXPECTED. Almost nothing needed deleting. 396 of 406 cross-book pairs and 508 of 615 cross-facet pairs came back genuinely different claims. The real defect was that claims were filed under the wrong section heading, so unrelated claims ended up side by side looking like copies. And the reason for THAT turned out to be a design flaw rather than sloppy authoring: the colour family literally named 'signs' contains only 'warning', so anyone filing a deficiency SIGN is pulled toward it, while the correct home sits in the 'science' family. Worse, 'warning' is pinned second on the page, so the misfiled claim gets promoted ABOVE its correct twin. That is mechanically why those two cards ended up next to each other on his screen. I deliberately did NOT build the obvious gate. Forcing one facet per claim kind would demand 941 re-facets, 41.8% of the corpus, and would be wrong: a 'definition' claim legitimately spans thirteen facets, because 'Where does niobium get its name?' and 'Where is sulfur stored in the body?' are the same kind and belong in different sections. A gate that has to be wrong 941 times to be satisfied is not a gate, it is a wish with teeth. TWO CLAIMS WERE STATING DOSES THAT ARE NOWHERE IN THE BOOK THEY CITE. Not invented -- contaminated. One asserted selenium at 1,000-3,000 mcg a day and displayed that figure in its reader-facing answer; an exhaustive search of all 1.17 million characters of Rare Earths found it zero times, and found it instead in Dead Doctors. The other asserted chromium's body burden and a USDA prevalence figure absent from all 692,000 characters of Hell's Kitchen and present in four other books. Both are real Wallach, attributed to the wrong source. Both trimmed. I CORRUPTED SIX DOSE NUMBERS MYSELF AND CAUGHT IT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. Joining OCR line-break hyphens in the newly widened quotes, my pattern matched digits as well as letters, so '800-\n1200' collapsed into '8001200' across six vitamin E doses, plus two vitamin B designations and two year ranges. The project's own gate pattern is letters-only; I had written a looser one. I found it by reading what the script actually did rather than trusting that it worked, reverted the book sources through git, and re-ran it with the pattern narrowed to match the gate. Nothing reached a seal. This is precisely the class the source rule exists to prevent, and it was my error, not one I inherited. The guards earned their keep repeatedly. A tool refused an entire book rather than orphan a mapped condition. My own sync guard aborted rather than silently overwrite 57 corrected quotes with the older narrower ones. The OCR sweep skipped Asa Chandler and thirteen instances of Kazuhiko Asai that a naive replace would have mangled. And after the deletions a gate found a THIRD place a claim id can live -- a hand-authored mechanism file where selenium's rendered quote pointed at a claim I had just removed. The standing lesson said a purge is two deletions. It is three. Board 89/89, corpus sealed at 469, 2,230 claims, three seals all authorised individually. Still open and named rather than buried: 46 more question collisions across 93 claims, which is the same twin-card symptom corpus-wide and now has a workflow running against it.

## 2026-08-06 12:17 UTC-05:00 · round-close · corpus/un-saveable-list
Swept all 2,250 claims for more superseded dose ceilings after yesterday's vitamin D deletions. Found exactly one survivor -- and it did not need deleting. Zero claims removed.
  ↳ Yesterday three claims were deleted for telling readers to cap vitamin D at 400 IU a day, against the 1,000-2,000 IU his newest book gives. This was the obvious follow-up: how many more are hiding? The answer turned out to be one, and the honest fix was not deletion. The claim summarised a whole page of the book but only quoted the bottom of it, and the bad number lived in the un-quoted part -- so trimming the summary back to what its own quote actually says removed the 400 IU limit without losing a single word Wallach really wrote. A second claim looked identical and was the exact opposite: its quote had been cut too SHORT, and trimming it would have destroyed a real angina protocol. That one got its full passage back instead. WHAT THE SWEEP ACTUALLY DID. 2,250 claims, four overlapping passes: a wide net for ceiling language (485), a tightening to bound-word-near-a-number (57, all read), an entity-anchored pass requiring the bound word to GOVERN a named essential (120, all read), and every contraindication and toxicity_sign read regardless (73). Plus a complete enumeration of all 50 vitamin-D claims. Both detectors were negative-controlled against the three already-deleted claims: 3/3 caught. The first entity pass was thrown away -- it scored 461 with 'histidine' on top, because the canon stores the 3-letter amino abbreviation and 'His' matched every 'His treatment...'. That is the same stemming noise the last session recorded, hit again from a new angle. THE RESULT, AND WHY IT IS SMALL. Only one numeric ceiling in the whole corpus still sits below its essential's current target. Two other candidates dissolved on reading: one is a deficiency FLOOR, not a ceiling, and the other attributes its 15 mcg selenium limit to Pauling and refutes it in the same breath. There is a structural reason the list is this short, and it is checkable rather than a hunch: nearly every 1995-to-2014 target moved DOWN (molybdenum 500 to 10-25 mcg, vanadium 500 to 50-100, iron 45 to 15-30). Vitamin D is the only essential whose number rose sharply. An old ceiling can only contradict a new target when the target went UP, so vitamin D was structurally the only place this could happen at all. A DECISION I HAD TO REVERSE MID-TASK. I presented the angina claim as the same prose-overreach defect and Luneth approved trimming it. Then reading the book at its offset showed the entire ANGINA entry sitting immediately before the quoted slice -- the write-up was faithful and the QUOTE was too narrow. Trimming would have deleted chelation-over-bypass, calcium 2,000 mg, magnesium 800 mg, EFA and hawthorn to remove a numberless sentence we are keeping in another claim anyway. I stopped and re-asked rather than executing the approved-but-now-wrong instruction, and he chose to widen. A TOOL THAT WAS ABOUT TO WRECK A FILE. vb_apply.py had indent=2 hardcoded while the draft it edits is indent=1. One verbatim edit would have re-spaced all 510 claims, and the seal would have promoted that reformat onto the golden shard -- burying a 2-line change in roughly 40,000. That is the identical failure fixed in two sibling tools on 2026-08-05; this one was missed. It now measures before writing, and measures BEFORE mutating (afterwards the original bytes cannot be reproduced). Actual sealed-shard diff for both claim edits: 3 insertions, 4 deletions. The per-book indent list in memory was wrong again, in a third direction. Measured: lets-play-doctor is indent=1, not the sole indent=2. Three drafts reproduce at no indent at all, because they are indent=1 with CRLF while the check compares LF-joined output -- both sanctioned edit tools will now refuse to write those three. The refusal is correct and fail-safe; the message was misleading, so it now names CRLF when it sees it. A GATE THAT WENT RED BECAUSE OF THE FIX. Widening the angina quote made it span five OCR line-wrap hyphens the short slice was too small to contain, so frontface_verbatims_clean reddened. That is the documented trap -- on a post-fix red, ask what was making it pass before. The answer was 'the quote was too small to contain the defect'. Fixed at source, scoped to that span only, CRLF preserved, and 'coronary by-pass' deliberately left because it is the book's real mid-line hyphenation rather than a wrap. WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. The board is 89/89 and that means nothing drifted, not that anything is right -- 23 of the 89 gates bear on truth outside our own files. render_probe_search fails, and I proved it was already failing at HEAD by stashing the whole working tree and re-running it there, rather than assuming. The sweep also surfaced a larger defect class I did NOT fix: at least 86 claims state a figure in their write-up that is absent from their own quote. 86 is a floor with a known false-negative mode -- my own counter wrongly cleared the vitamin D claim, because it tolerates twice-daily halving and 400 matched the 200 inside '75-200 mg'. No gate was written, because the rule needs Luneth's call on legitimate restatement versus overreach, and inventing it would be a WISH dressed as a gate. One coverage hole is named rather than hidden: with the twin deleted and this one trimmed, the corpus now carries no heart-disease PREVENTION protocol, only post-heart-attack treatment.

One of his notes is worth keeping as a principle. About a lithium panel he said it was highly engaging but left him feeling he could never stop supplementing for the rest of his life. Engaging and still a failure. How a panel leaves the reader is the test, not whether it holds attention. TECHNICAL RECORD. 76 quotes across 18 *demos*.html moved onto the live div.ds-pull-quote-wrap.kd-ep-fam__quote > blockquote.ds-pull-quote > p + footer (entity-page.ts:1034); 85 bespoke .xxx-quote rules deleted. ## 2026-08-03 13:24 UTC-05:00 · round-close · engine/pinned-browser
Pinned the browser the dashboard is frozen against — Ungoogled Chromium, no updater at all — and ruled file:// permanent. The leak test's first version said 'no leaks'; it was blind.
  ↳ Two questions closed for good, and one browser installed. Luneth ruled that this app must always open in any browser, from a plain file on disk. That rules out ever packaging it as a desktop application. Electron was genuinely better on most of the measures we compared - it would have removed the reason the bundle is 12 MB, and lifted the 5 MB storage ceiling the code already warns about - but it loses on the one thing that matters most: an app dies with its shell. Static files outlive the browser. If the frozen browser ever stops working on some future Windows, the dashboard still opens, and the user's health data is not hostage to a binary. Tauri was worse still: it ships no engine, and on Windows borrows Microsoft's, which Microsoft updates on the user's machine - the exact failure this project exists to prevent. The engine is Ungoogled Chromium. It has no updater at all, rather than one we switch off, and it severs its ties to Google in the source - Google's domains are rewritten to an address that does not exist and then blocked outright. It was downloaded, its fingerprint checked against the published one BEFORE anything was unpacked, and it is now pinned so we would know if a single byte changed. THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING. I wrote a test to prove the browser stays inside its own folder and writes nothing to the machine. It printed NO LEAKS DETECTED. That was false. The test compared the NAMES of registry entries, and the relevant entry already existed on this machine, so anything written INSIDE it was invisible to the test by construction. I then checked the timestamp on that entry, saw it was from 2024, and nearly reported the browser clean twice over - but a registry timestamp only covers its own level, and the write had landed one level deeper. Only when the test was rewritten to compare the VALUES themselves did it immediately find the write. This is the same lesson as the write-primitive fix earlier today, arriving from a different direction: a clean result from an instrument that cannot see the thing it is looking for is not evidence, and it is far more dangerous than a red one, because it ends the search. What it found is small and benign - Chromium stores tamper-detection fingerprints of its own settings there, no personal data, nothing that leaves the machine, and no documented way to move it. Everything else stayed inside the folder, including the crash-handler leak the spec had specifically feared, which did not happen. But "small and benign" is Luneth's call to make, not mine, so no document claims the engine is fully self-contained until he rules on it. TECHNICAL RECORD Decisions: chronicle/decisions/2026-08-03-file-protocol-is-sacred.md, -orphaned-log-entry.md, -pinned-engine-acquisition.md. The first records the taxes the ruling knowingly accepts (no runtime fetch(), the ~5 MB localStorage ceiling, no secure-context APIs) as consequences rather than defects, so a future session does not re-litigate them as bugs. Engine: ungoogled-chromium 151.0.7922.71-1.1 windows x64, archive sha256 f49303e9b61aab63... verified before extraction, 76 files / 436,216,729 B extracted to engine/, gitignored and confirmed invisible to git via git check-ignore. The pin lives in the committed engine-manifest.json; the bytes live beside it. run-dashboard.bat launches with --user-data-dir, --disable-machine-id, --disable-encryption and --app (a chrome-less window, so it looks like an app while staying file://). New gate pinned_engine_integrity (external): file count, total bytes and chrome.exe sha256 against the manifest, with engine/ absent a DECLARED skip rather than a silent pass. Negative-controlled against five planted defects - swapped binary, changed byte total, added file, gutted hash, gutted version - red on all five, and the manifest restored byte-exact afterwards. Fixed safe_write, the primitive every write in this project depends on: it silently rewrote line endings and its own verify could not see it — and neither could the gate built to catch exactly that.
  ↳ Every file change in this project goes through one tool. That tool had a flaw it was structurally unable to notice. When it saved a file it quietly changed the invisible marks that end each line, and when it read the file back it changed them again in the opposite direction. Its own "did this save correctly?" check compared those two equally-altered copies, so it answered yes no matter what was really on the disk. Three things followed from that. It converted files to a different line-ending style without being asked, which is why 554 files in this project now sit in a style the repository itself does not store. It could never convert a file the other way, because the fix was undone by the very save that was meant to apply it -- so an earlier session was told a save succeeded when it had changed nothing whatsoever. And the sizes it reported were counts of characters while the message said bytes, which is very likely what made that session read a real, successful write as a no-op. The part worth remembering is the second discovery. There was already an alarm whose entire job was to prove this tool writes exactly what it is handed. It had been green for months. It read the file back with a low-level call that, on Windows, silently applies the very same alteration as the save -- so it was auditing the tool using the tool's own blind spot. It was filed under the one category of check this project says can catch a value that is wrong but consistent with our own files, and it could not have caught this. A check that shares the defect it is testing is not a check. So the alarm was repaired first, and deliberately run against the still-broken tool to watch it fail, before the tool was touched at all. Otherwise "it passes now" would have proved nothing. TECHNICAL RECORD tools/safe_write.py -- Path.read_text / Path.write_text default to newline=None, i.e. Python's translated-newline space: LF -> CRLF on write and CRLF -> LF on read. The round trip was symmetric, so the `landed != new_content` verify compared two translated strings. All disk I/O now routes through two new functions, _read_exact and _write_exact (raw bytes plus an explicit UTF-8 codec), which are the only places the module touches file content -- translation cannot be reintroduced by a future edit without deleting them outright. The step-5 verify and the post-swap readback compare bytes and print a line-ending census next to the sizes, because equal LENGTHS never implied equal content. safe_replace, safe_append, check_file, _read_payload are byte-exact; --payload-stdin reads sys.stdin.buffer. Returned sizes are true byte counts. Because matching is now byte-exact, an LF payload will not match a CRLF file. That failure is deliberate and loud: a new _newline_hint names line endings as the cause and says which style to restage with, and stays silent on a genuine content miss. `check <path>` now prints a file's ending census so a caller can stage correctly in the first place. tools/invariants.py -- _read_via_os now passes | O_BINARY. On Windows os.open defaults to TEXT mode, so os.read translated CRLF to LF; the gate's "independent" readback applied the same transformation as the write. check_safe_write_canary now compares raw bytes, carries LF, CRLF, a lone CR and non-ASCII in its probe payload, and asserts the reported size is a true byte count. NEW GATE board_claims_match_reality (consistency) -- CLAUDE.md's "what a green board actually means" section retyped the gate total and the external-anchor count that invariants.py computes: a canonical value in two hand-maintained places, which section 00.B rule 1 forbids. It had already rotted -- the doctor sweep added two gates and the contract kept saying 85 / ~21 while the board ran 87 / 23. The gate reddens on a mismatch AND on a reworded claim, so it can never go green by losing its subject. NEW tools/test_safe_write_byte_exact.py -- 16 cases. Three are load-bearing: they re-break the primitive on purpose (a translating write, caught by the byte verify; a symmetric translation that corrupts the intent too, caught by intent_check; a character-count return, caught by the size assertion) and assert the canary goes red each time. A test that only showed today's code working would have passed just as happily on the broken version. Docs reconciled in the same patch: CLAUDE.md 85->88 gates and ~21->23 external; the write-discipline skill's "Known defect in the primitive" section replaced by the byte-exact contract, with rule 4 and Windows quirk 3 rewritten (payloads match the TARGET's endings, not always LF); chronicle/next-chunk.md no longer carries this as the open bug. VERIFIED. Pre-fix negative controls reproduced all three recorded symptoms: a pure-LF payload landed CRLF and reported 17 for a 20-byte file; a CRLF->LF repair returned OK having changed zero bytes; a lone CR produced "intended=3B landed=3B" on a failing check. The re-codified canary went RED against the broken primitive ("intended=136B landed=136B") and GREEN after ("byte-exact round-trip OK (140B; LF, CRLF and lone CR all preserved)"). board_claims_match_reality went RED against the stale contract ("doc says 85, board runs 88; doc says 21, board has 23") and GREEN after. test_safe_write_byte_exact 16/16, exit 0. node tools/build.mjs exit 0. invariants 88/88, zero reds -- 23 external, 23 consistency, 40 structural, 2 meta. LEFT FOR LUNETH. 554 working-tree files are CRLF only because this bug made them so; git stores LF for every one of them (core.autocrlf=input), and .gitattributes records that this same mechanism already broke the design-system.css seal once. It was also the concrete mechanism behind the design ceiling - 250 KB gzipped rules out motion, lottie and d3 before a single design decision is made. WHAT REPLACED IT. THE DISCRIMINATOR, and why it is not book_purity's. book_purity asks "are BOTH halves real words?" and reviews if so. Correct for a whole-book sweep, wrong here: it sends de-|spite and mal-|absorption to review because de, mal, spite and absorption are all words, when the answers are obviously despite and malabsorption. The sharper question for a LINE-BREAK wrap is whether the REJOINED token is itself a real word: try+ing -> trying joins; potassium+rich -> potassiumrich does not. book_purity's two hard KEEP rules (chemical/stereo prefix, proper-noun second half) were inherited unchanged and override the join. WHY THIS WAS SAFE TO DO BEFORE THE VISION PASS. De-hyphenation is orthogonal to OCR correctness — it removes a typesetting artifact and cannot create, hide or worsen a letter error. It is also self-protecting: if OCR corrupted either half, the rejoin almost never yields a real word, so it lands in KEEP/REVIEW rather than JOIN. The converse is the load-bearing caveat: a KEEP verdict is NEGATIVE evidence and is only as good as its input. WAL-CLM-RARE-000336's pro-|side was ruled "a real compound" purely because the page's "vide" had been OCR'd to "side" — it is not a compound, the page says provide.
